title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
description: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. If A is an n×n matrix with characteristic polynomial p(λ) = det(λI - A), then p(A) = 0.

overview.historicalContext:
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem is named after Arthur Cayley (1821-1895) and William Rowan Hamilton (1805-1865). Hamilton first proved a version for quaternions in 1853, while Cayley stated the theorem for matrices in 1858, though he only verified specific cases. The first complete proof for arbitrary matrices was given by Ferdinand Frobenius in 1878.

The theorem is fundamental to linear algebra and has applications in control theory, differential equations, and quantum mechanics. It shows that every matrix is a root of a polynomial of bounded degree, which has profound implications for computing matrix functions.
overview.problemStatement:
Theorem (Cayley-Hamilton): If A is an n×n matrix over a commutative ring, and p(λ) = det(λI - A) is its characteristic polynomial, then:

$$p(A) = A^n - c_{n-1}A^{n-1} - \cdots - c_1A - c_0I = 0$$

where the c_i are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof in Mathlib uses a clever algebraic approach. The key insight is the identity relating the adjugate matrix to the determinant:

$$A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = \det(A) \cdot I$$

By working with matrices over the polynomial ring and carefully manipulating the adjugate of (XI - A), the proof shows that evaluating the characteristic polynomial at A yields zero.

The beauty of this approach is that it's purely algebraic and works over any commutative ring, not just fields.
keyInsights: The characteristic polynomial encodes all eigenvalues (with multiplicity) as its roots
Cayley-Hamilton implies that A^n can be expressed as a linear combination of I, A, A², ..., A^(n-1)
When det(A) ≠ 0, the inverse A⁻¹ can be written as a polynomial in A
For 2×2 matrices: A² - trace(A)·A + det(A)·I = 0, giving the explicit inverse formula
The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial, so its degree is at most n

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Overview of the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, its historical context, and the approach using Mathlib.
sections.mathContext: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem: every $n \times n$ matrix $A$ over a commutative ring satisfies its own characteristic polynomial $\chi_A(A) = 0$, where $\chi_A(t) = \det(tI - A)$.

sections.title: The Characteristic Polynomial
sections.summary: Definition and properties of the characteristic polynomial: monic and degree equals dimension.
sections.mathContext: $\chi_A(t) = \det(tI - A)$ is monic of degree $n$ for $A \in M_n(R)$. In Lean: `Matrix.charpoly A` computes $\chi_A$. Key properties: `charpoly_monic` (leading coefficient 1) and `charpoly_natDegree` (degree = $n$).

sections.title: The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
sections.summary: The main theorem statement: every matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial.
sections.mathContext: $\chi_A(A) = 0$ in $M_n(R)$, i.e., substituting the matrix $A$ into its characteristic polynomial $\chi_A(t) = t^n - \text{tr}(A)t^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n\det(A)$ gives the zero matrix. In Lean: `Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly A = 0`.

sections.title: Examples
sections.summary: Concrete examples: identity matrix, nilpotent matrices, scalar matrices, zero matrix.
sections.mathContext: Identity: $\chi_I(t) = (t-1)^n$, so $\chi_I(I) = (I-I)^n = 0$. Scalar: $\chi_{cI}(t) = (t-c)^n$. Nilpotent: if $A^k = 0$, then $\chi_A(t) = t^n$ (all eigenvalues 0). Zero: $\chi_0(t) = t^n$, $\chi_0(0) = 0^n = 0$.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.summary: Applications: polynomial annihilation, bounds on matrix dimension.
sections.mathContext: Every $n \times n$ matrix is annihilated by a polynomial of degree $\leq n$. The minimal polynomial $\mu_A(t)$ divides $\chi_A(t)$ (by Cayley-Hamilton), so $\deg(\mu_A) \leq n$. This means $\{I, A, A^2, \ldots, A^{n-1}\}$ spans all powers of $A$.

sections.title: The 2x2 Case
sections.summary: The explicit formula for 2x2 matrices and connection to trace and determinant.
sections.mathContext: For $A \in M_2(R)$: $A^2 - \text{tr}(A) \cdot A + \det(A) \cdot I = 0$. When $\det(A) \neq 0$: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)}(\text{tr}(A) \cdot I - A)$, expressing the inverse as a polynomial in $A$.

sections.title: Theoretical Significance
sections.summary: Why Cayley-Hamilton matters: applications to linear algebra, control theory, and eigenvalue theory.
sections.mathContext: Applications: (1) Matrix exponential: $e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \alpha_k(t) A^k$ (reduce infinite series to degree $< n$). (2) Control theory: reachability of $\dot{x} = Ax + Bu$ determined by $[B, AB, \ldots, A^{n-1}B]$. (3) Jordan form: $\chi_A$ factors over $\overline{R}$ give eigenvalue structure.

conclusion.summary: This formalization demonstrates the Cayley-Hamilton theorem using Mathlib's algebraic approach. The theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial, a fundamental result with far-reaching applications.
conclusion.implications: The theorem has important implications for computing matrix functions, analyzing linear dynamical systems, and understanding the algebraic structure of matrix rings. It shows that n×n matrices form a space of 'polynomial dimension' n.
openQuestions: What is the minimal polynomial of a given matrix, and how does it relate to the characteristic polynomial?
How can Cayley-Hamilton be used to efficiently compute matrix exponentials e^(At)?
What is the analog of Cayley-Hamilton for infinite-dimensional operators?

crossReferences.description: The FTA guarantees that the characteristic polynomial of a complex matrix factors completely, enabling eigenvalue decomposition — Cayley-Hamilton provides the algebraic framework

Both connect polynomial algebra to structural results: Abel-Ruffini shows quintic polynomials can't be solved by radicals, Cayley-Hamilton shows matrices are annihilated by their characteristic polynomials
